sections.text: Every value in Rust has a type. Scalar types hold a single value: integers, floating-point numbers, booleans and characters.

Integers are whole numbers. Signed types (i8, i16, i32, i64, i128) can be negative; unsigned types (u8, u16, u32, u64, u128) can't. The number is the size in bits, which sets the range: a u8 holds 0 to 255 and an i8 holds -128 to 127. i32 is the default. usize is used for counts and indexes.
The _ in 1_250 is just for readability, like a comma in 1,250.
Floats are f64 (the default) and f32. bool is true or false. char is a single Unicode character in single quotes:
Dividing two integers drops the remainder, so 7 / 2 is 3. Use floats when you need the fraction.
Rust never mixes number types on its own. You can't multiply an integer by a float, even when the answer seems obvious. Convert the integer to a float first with as:
items as f64 turns the integer 3 into the float 3.0, so both sides of * are f64 and the program prints 7.5.
Between number types, as never fails, but it can lose information when the value doesn't fit the new type:

2.9 as i32 is 2, because the fraction is dropped. 300 is too big for a u8, and an integer cast keeps only the bits that fit, so it wraps around to 300 - 256 = 44. (A float is different: 300.0 as u8 gives 255, the biggest u8.) Only use as when you know the value fits. It doesn't work on text, so use parse() to turn text into a number.

Coming from another language: there are no automatic number conversions in Rust, not even from i32 to i64. If an integer overflows while the program runs, it stops with an error. That's what happens in this app and in cargo run (a debug build). Release builds skip that check and wrap around silently, unless you turn overflow checks on.
Coming from another language: for conversions that can never lose data, use i64::from(x) (or x.into()) instead of as. They only compile when every possible value fits, like i32 to i64.

Coming from another language: number literals can carry a type suffix, like 5u8 or 2.5f32. usize is as wide as a pointer, so 64 bits on most machines today. A char is 4 bytes and holds one Unicode scalar value (a code point). Some things that look like one character, such as flag emoji or accented letters built from two code points, need more than one char.

exercise.prompt: This program doesn't compile because total is a float and count is an integer, and Rust won't divide one by the other. Convert count to f64 with as so it prints: 2.5
hints: Rust needs both sides of / to be the same type. Find where count is used in the division.
Write as f64 straight after count, right where it's divided. as happens before /, so you don't need brackets.
Change the division to total / count as f64. Only count needs the conversion, because total is already a float.
